articles.title: Old Al Michaels stumbles through awkward Lake America-Trump jab during Thursday Night Football broadcast
articles.summary: Al Michaels dropped a smug Trump joke about Lake Ontario's renaming during Thursday Night Football, leaving Kirk Herbstreit frozen in silence.
articles.body: Thursday Night Football on Amazon Prime is already an endurance test. Between brutal offensive line play, endless commercials and whatever disaster the Cleveland Browns are trotting out, sitting through four quarters takes serious grit. Throw in 81-year-old Al Michaels auditioning for late-night TV over an aerial shot of Cleveland, and watching him crash and burn in real time is pure banana land. Coming back from commercial during the Browns-Patriots game, Uncle Al dropped his cutting-edge political commentary on Donald Trump’s executive order renaming Lake Ontario to "Lake America" amid the ongoing U.S.-Canada trade war. TRUMP FLOATS RENAMING THE ATLANTIC AND PACIFIC OCEANS AFTER REBRANDING HISTORIC LAKE "That is Lake Erie. We think it is still called Lake Erie ... We're not quite sure at this point. But we'll be by Lake something like Ontario or whatever it's going to be called by the time we get to Buffalo. Anyway, you know what I'm talking about ... Read the news." WATCH: Oof. You could physically feel the oxygen get sucked out of the booth. Kirk Herbstreit, a guy who carefully tiptoes around political landmines so he can host "College GameDay" in peace, completely froze. Herbie sat there like a hostage before mumbling under his breath: "Some of us know ..." Translation: Al, please. Do not drag me into your country club Resistance Twitter jokes. Al Michaels is a broadcasting legend. Miracle on Ice, manning the booth for 11 Super Bowls, all of it. But watching old Al try landing a smug Trump jab on live TV hits with the force of a wet paper towel. It’s classic boomer-broadcaster energy, like your blue-haired cousin dropping political riffs at Thanksgiving. Maybe Uncle Al wasn't feeling particularly patriotic with New England in town. DEBUT OF FORMER STEELERS COACH MIKE TOMLIN ON NBC SNF HAD HIGHLIGHT MOMENTS BUT WAS TOO CAREFUL AND REHEARSED Or maybe he spent his pregame prep doom-scrolling political Twitter in his trailer. Imagine the Cleveland Browns dropping 27 first-half points and the worst part of the entire night is still Al Michaels forcing his anti-Trump tight-five on the audience. Absolute fever dream on Amazon Prime. "Read the news," Al smugly instructed at the end of his bit. How about we stick to calling the game, Al? CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP If he attempts another political tightrope walk like that, Amazon might just pull the plug and swap him out for A.I. Michaels for the rest of the season. At least the digital version stays on script. Leave the monologues to the late-night guys, and let Herbie live to see Saturday. articles.title: Fired Stars and Stripes journalists sue Trump administration for censorship
articles.summary: Staff at the military newspaper allege US government sought to violate First Amendment rights to free speech.
articles.body:
Three staff members from the Stars and Stripes military newspaper have filed a lawsuit against the United States Department of Defense, alleging that their recent firing was part of an effort to erode the paper’s independence.

In Thursday’s court filings, the newspaper’s publisher Max Lederer, editor-in-chief Erik Slavin and Middle East reporter Lara Korte argued that their First Amendment rights to free speech had been infringed.

The Stars and Stripes has long billed itself as an independent source for military news, though it receives government funding for its operations.

But last week, the three journalists received notices of termination from the Pentagon that reportedly accused them of insubordination.

That has raised questions about the Defense Department’s longtime commitment to respecting the newspaper’s editorial independence.

Thursday’s complaint accuses the department and several of its leaders, including Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth , of engaging in “extraordinary censorship efforts”.

“Defendants are attempting to fire Plaintiffs for speaking up as private citizens in support of the press’s freedom to cover military operations,” the lawsuit says.

“This [legal] action seeks to prevent the blatant violation of the First Amendment rights of these journalists.”

The case is set to be heard in a district court in Washington, DC.

Korte explained the journalists’ reason for filing the lawsuit in a social media post .

“Everyone deserves the right to a free and independent press, especially our service members,” she wrote. “This lawsuit is about safeguarding the mission of Stars and Stripes journalists so they can continue to do their jobs without fear or retaliation.”

The legal battle is the latest instance under President Donald Trump of the executive branch being sued for allegedly penalising reporters and media personalities who do not comply with the administration’s viewpoints.

The lawsuit points to a July interview on CBS Sunday Morning as the “genesis” of the friction between the Stars and Stripes journalists and the Trump administration.

Both Korte and Slavin were featured in the segment. A reporter for the morning news show asked them about their work and recent statements from the Pentagon indicating it would seek to redirect the newspaper’s focus.

“You have a sign on your desk: Pick your battles,” CBS News reporter David Martin asked Slavin. “Which foxholes are you willing to die in?”

“We need to be able to provide independent news to service members,” Slavin responded. “If we can’t do that, if we were turned into something other than that, if we were public relations, that’s the foxhole.”

The CBS interview followed a statement in January, in which Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said his department would return Stars and Stripes “to its original mission: reporting for our warfighters”.

“We will modernize its operations, refocus its content away from woke distractions that syphon morale, and adapt it to serve a new generation of service members,” Parnell wrote.

“It will focus on warfighting, weapons systems, fitness, lethality, survivability, and ALL THINGS MILITARY.”

But critics have denounced the modernisation initiative as a smokescreen through which the Pentagon is seeking to reshape the Stars and Stripes’ coverage.

The lawsuit points to the newspaper’s key role in breaking coverage about deteriorating conditions on board the USS Abraham Lincoln, an aircraft carrier that has been on deployment, without a port stop, since November of last year.

The Stars and Stripes was one of the first media outlets to cover the supply shortages on the ship, as well as the mental health struggles of the sailors working through the record-long deployment.

But Trump and Hegseth have both denied reports of poor living conditions on the USS Lincoln, calling such news “fake”.

The lawsuit suggests the recent firings may be retaliation for the Stars and Stripes reporting on the subject.

A day after one of its articles was published, the lawsuit alleges that the Defense Department contacted Lederer, the publisher, about firing Korte and Slavin. The department allegedly pointed to the CBS interview from weeks earlier as justification.

Lederer did not follow through with the order to deliver the termination notices. Instead, he announced his intention to retire in September.

His memo to the Stars and Stripes staff suggested he had disagreements with the “direction the leadership of the Department of Defense has for the organization”.

But on August 21, the Department of Defense had issued termination notices to all three employees, including Lederer.

In April, the newspaper’s ombudsman, Jacqueline Smith, was also fired. Her role, in part, was charged with safeguarding the independence of the Stars and Stripes, a newspaper with a storied history, stretching back to the US Civil War.

Korte has worked at the paper since 2024. Her colleagues Slavin and Lederer have been with the Stars and Stripes for 21 and 25 years, respectively.

“Defense officials and military commanders have long made clear that Stripes would not be subject to interference by military officials,” the lawsuit says.

“Stripes’ historical editorial independence is critical to its core mission of gathering and providing unbiased, credible journalism to the US military community.”

articles.title: US nears deal to secure stake in Venezuelan oil fields, insiders say
articles.summary: Pact with Caracas would bolster US oil supplies for years to come, but may face legal challenges.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump’s administration is working on a deal to lock in long-term access to some of Venezuela’s crude reserves, Reuters sources have said.

The agreement, which insiders said could be signed and made public soon, is expected to operate in a way that would let the US government secure a group of Venezuelan oilfields to be developed by American companies, with the resulting supply guaranteed for the US.

“This is real and being discussed at the highest levels of the US and Venezuelan governments,” one of the sources said.

A separate source said a “lease” was in consideration as the legal model to make the deal work, with a further auction or tender to allocate each one of the fields among US producers.

A list of 17 fields in negotiation seen by Reuters includes green fields in the vast Orinoco Belt, combined with mature areas in Lake Maracaibo, some of which are currently operated by a small Chinese firm whose contract was signed during the administration of former President Nicolas Maduro.

The White House referred questions to the US Department of Energy. Venezuela’s oil ministry, state oil company PDVSA and the Energy Department did not immediately reply to requests for comment. Venezuelan oil minister Paula Henao could not be reached for comment.

Caracas is considering leaving the OPEC oil production group as it strengthens ties with the US, Bloomberg reported on Thursday. Venezuela, which joined the group as a founding member in 1960, has not met OPEC quotas for years as its state-run oil industry suffered from neglect and corruption. Washington has long been at odds with OPEC for its influence on oil prices.

Current hydrocarbons regulation in Venezuela, which has the world’s largest crude reserves, does not include acreage leases for oil areas, while the constitution reserves the industry’s core activities to the state.

Recently reformed oil legislation allows oilfield operation through joint ventures and production-sharing contracts. The Venezuelan government has for decades prevented foreign producers from booking the country’s oil reserves.

While full details of the prospective deal between Washington and Caracas have yet to emerge, it could raise constitutional questions and face legal challenges, according to experts.

Since the US captured and removed former President Nicolas Maduro from power in January, Washington has been trying to secure a stable flow of Venezuelan crude for US refineries while promoting American investment into the country’s deteriorated energy industry, which currently produces some 1.25 million barrels per day of crude.

The Trump administration is under pressure ahead of November’s midterm elections over rising petrol prices , which could be eased through cheaper oil supplies and expanded output. The US has also been looking for solutions to replenish its Strategic Petroleum Reserve, the oil stockpile it keeps for emergencies, including the possibility of crude swaps with US producers.

Funding shortages and ongoing maintenance at the reserve have limited the administration’s efforts to refill it after the US tapped it following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and then again after the war on Iran was launched in February.

articles.title: Archaeologists Solve Dorset’s 7-Year Mystery After Discovering a Medieval Farmstead Beneath Walls That Once Had No Explanation
articles.summary: Rest of World News: A field in Dorset that had puzzled archaeologists for the best part of a decade has finally given up its secret. Bournemouth University academic Dr De.
articles.body: A field in Dorset that had puzzled archaeologists for the best part of a decade has finally given up its secret. Bournemouth University academic Dr Derek Pitman first came across substantial walls hidden beneath the ground during a student training excavation back in 2018, but at the time there simply was not enough evidence to say what the walls belonged to, how old they were, or who might once have lived there. The question stayed with him for seven years, until he assembled a much larger team, made up of specialists from Bournemouth University, Forestry England, Wessex Archaeology, the National Trust and TCMS Heritage, to reopen the dig.That renewed effort has paid off, with the structure now believed to be a farmstead already recorded on a fifteenth century map of the local area. The find also sits within a much wider stretch of historic activity around Poole Harbour, and the full excavation story will be told in a new documentary due for release this week.How archaeologists identified the Dorset farmsteadAccording to Bournemouth University, Pitman led a new team back to the same Dorset field to reopen the investigation. The project drew together archaeologists and heritage specialists from Bournemouth University itself, Forestry England, Wessex Archaeology, the National Trust and TCMS Heritage, giving the dig a breadth of experience the 2018 excavation simply did not have.According to Bournemouth University, the structure is now believed to be a farmstead, one that had originally been recorded on a local fifteenth century map of the area. What had been an unexplained tangle of walls in 2018 could finally be placed within a documented historical record, with the field's location now thought to match the site shown on the old map.How the farmstead fits into Poole Harbour’s historyFor Pitman, the farmstead is not just an isolated find but a window into a much longer story of human activity in the area. He pointed out that the field sits within an extraordinary archaeological landscape on the edge of Poole Harbour, a landscape where people have lived, worked and drawn on its resources for centuries.What elevates the discovery beyond a single set of walls. The farmstead now sits alongside evidence of centuries of human settlement and resource use around Poole Harbour, suggesting the field was never an isolated curiosity but part of a continuously occupied and exploited stretch of countryside stretching through generations.Why archaeologists are turning the Dorset discovery into a documentaryPitman and a colleague have chosen to document the process for the public. Dr Lawrence Shaw, a Bournemouth University Visiting Fellow and Lead Historic Environment Advisor at Forestry England, worked alongside Pitman to prepare a documentary covering the excavation and its findings.The documentary is set to give viewers a closer look at how the mystery was finally solved. According to Bournemouth University, the film is scheduled for release on their YouTube channel, Career in Ruins, and aims to explore both the archaeological process itself and the challenges the team faced along the way, offering a behind-the-scenes account of how a seven-year-old question was finally answered.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Six months on, Trump’s Iran ‘excursion’ risks igniting crises far beyond the Middle East
articles.summary: When US President Donald Trump launched his war against Iran, he called it an “excursion” that would take just a few weeks. Six months later, the conflict has become a nightmare for almost everyone even remotely involved in it.
articles.body: When US President Donald Trump launched his war against Iran, he called it an “excursion” that would take just a few weeks. Six months later, the conflict has become a nightmare for almost everyone even remotely involved in it. It’s been a disaster for the Iranian people, for the millions living elsewhere across the Middle East, and for consumers around the world who are struggling with higher costs. Yet Trump’s war goals remain unfulfilled, even though the goalposts keep shifting: from initially demanding a complete Iranian surrender, regime change and the abandoning of the Islamic Republic’s nuclear ambitions, to more recently simply demanding the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and putting the brakes on Tehran’s nuclear program. But the war’s unintended consequences have spread far beyond the Middle East, affecting global security, diminishing America’s global standing, and potentially providing its adversaries with an opportunity to expand their influence. As the Trump administration focuses all its energy on trying to get out of the self-inflicted crisis in Iran, it has taken the eye off the ball of other potential global flashpoints the US has long been involved in, including Ukraine, Taiwan and the South China Sea, and the Koreas. From Trump’s decision to scale back the annual joint military exercises with South Korea and pulling out the only US aircraft carrier in the Western Pacific, to the critical shortages of ballistic missile interceptors in Ukraine, many of the war’s most consequential geopolitical and security effects may ultimately be felt far beyond the Middle East, and have yet to materialize. Emily Harding, a vice president of the Defense and Security Department at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a US-based think tank, said that while none of the potential flashpoints have developed into a full-scale crisis yet, there is good reason to be worried. “This is the kind of thing where the global adversaries are going to be taking note of the situation and learning more about how the US reacts in certain moments and then folding that into their planning. But we haven’t seen anybody take advantage of it yet,” she said. “It’s more that some foundations are being weakened, not that we’re actually seeing the building start to shake.” Ukraine and Russia The US-Israeli attacks have sparked a furious retaliation from Tehran. Iranian drones, ballistic missiles and other projectiles have been raining down on US bases and allies across the Middle East. As the US and its allies burned through their weapons stockpiles, some ammunition originally slated for Ukraine had been redirected. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told CNN this month that his country had only a tenth of the interceptor missiles it urgently needed to stop surging Russian ballistic missile attacks. The shortages are having devastating consequences for the Ukrainians: This summer has been the deadliest period for civilians since May 2022. The global oil crisis caused by Iran’s decision to effectively shut the Strait of Hormuz has also undermined the Trump administration’s economic pressure campaign against Moscow. Faced with the rising cost of gasoline at US pumps, Trump took the controversial decision to lift some sanctions on Russian oil exports to cool the market. In doing so, the US effectively helped Russia earn more cash to fund the war effort in Ukraine. The global disruption to oil, gas and fertilizer trade caused by the closure of the strait has also helped Russia make inroads on finding new customers. Alexander Gabuev, the director of Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center in Berlin, said this was demonstrated when Russian President Vladimir Putin hosted the leaders of Southeast Asian countries in the Russian city of Kazan in June. “The turnout in Kazan was impressive: Nine of 11 heads of state from ASEAN were present, along with the Indonesian foreign minister and a special representative from Myanmar. Above all, these men decided to make the long journey to Russia because of US and Israeli attacks on Iran causing higher prices for energy and fertilizer,” he said. In some ways, the Iran war has benefited Ukraine. It has made the rest of the world realize that the more than four years of war have turned Kyiv into a drone superpower and led to an array of security cooperation agreements and ammunition promises with a number of nations. The Koreas The Iran war is now casting a shadow over another potential flashpoint: the Korean Peninsula, which has technically been at war for more than seven decades in the absence of a peace deal following the 1950-1953 conflict South and North Korea. The US has been deeply involved in the region, with some 28,500 American troops stationed in South Korea. But the decades-long relationship suffered a hiccup this year when Trump sharply curtailed the annual Ulchi Freedom Shield joint military exercises with Seoul, partly citing South Korea’s lack of support for the Iran war. The US president has also signaled openness for talks with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, who has been overseeing a steady increase in his country’s nuclear arsenal and regular missile launches. Analysts said the consequences of cutting military exercises impacts readiness if war were to resume on the Korean Peninsula in the short term, and its more distant effects include lengthening the time needed for Seoul to assume wartime control of its troops, something sought by both the South Koreans and the US. South Korean officials said this week that a second exercise, for amphibious landings scheduled for September, was canceled in June. Those exercises were to have involved US Marines stationed in the Japanese island of Okinawa, units of which were involved in the blockade of Iranian ports. There is also the question of supplies and logistics, including the reallocations of some US missile interceptors from South Korea to the Middle East during the fighting. The Pentagon hasn’t revealed how much of the interceptor inventory was moved, but analysts say possible long-term shortages of key interceptors like the Patriot system are likely. Taiwan and the South China Sea The deployment of the Japan-based aircraft carrier USS George Washington to the Arabian Sea to relieve the beleaguered USS Abraham Lincoln leaves the US without any aircraft carriers in the Pacific for an indeterminate time should the need for one arise. The US has had a continuous presence in the Pacific for more than two decades with the exception of a gap of several weeks in 2024. That lack of a carrier in the US 7th Fleet’s area of responsibility raises questions for other regional allies. The Philippines will be particularly worried given the increasing Chinese activity in the South China Sea, around disputed features like Scarborough Shoal, which lies in the Philippines exclusive economic zone but is effectively controlled by Beijing. Tensions between Manila and Beijing extend to Second Thomas Shoal which, like Scarborough, is in the Spratly Islands. Both have seen at-sea clashes between Filipino and Chinese personnel. The US and the Philippines have a mutual defense treaty, and if the tensions with China were to escalate, not having a carrier in the region could put US forces at a distinct disadvantage, especially given the current issues with munition stockpiles. “The big thing that I’m worried about is what it looks like for the US in a potential conflict with China,” Harding said. “We’re not seeing that turn up anytime soon … but if there were to be a conflict with China, we would be in a state of ammunition shortage, specifically the ones that we’re going to need for that conflict.” Global chokepoints There could be other devastating consequences of the war – for example if other players try to weaponize other international shipping chokepoints. “We’re not yet seeing this, but if it got to a point later on where one of those countries wanted to, they could certainly point to this as a (precedent),” Harding said. She added that the severity of the war’s impact will depend chiefly on how long the US keeps fighting it. “The Trump administration has to decide what’s good enough for an outcome here and if the only thing that’s good enough is a complete destruction of the nuclear program and, what Israel wants, which is an Iran that’s internally broken and divided, then that is a long commitment of both blood and treasure and the world economy is going to feel the consequences of that long term,” she said. But Trump could also decide that it could be enough to make the nuclear program “unusable,” she added – something he suggested could be done by keeping the key sites, currently destroyed and under the rubble, inaccessible to Iran by striking whenever Tehran tries to access them. “That’s not a great solution, but it’s a workable solution. And if that’s enough, and if (Iran’s) weakened proxy network is enough, then what you really have to deal with is the Strait of Hormuz, and that’s hard and a little bit expensive, but nowhere near as expensive as what (the US is) doing right now,” she said. “From the Iranian perspective, all they have to do is survive, and they’re doing that. So they can kind of keep this going for as long as they want.”

articles.title: China suspends flood rescue efforts near its border over ‘real possibility’ of secondary disaster
articles.summary: Hundreds have been killed in Wednesday’s catastrophic flash flooding. More than 1,300 people, including dozens of Americans, remain missing. Follow for live updates.
articles.body:
• Rescue suspended: China has suspended rescue efforts along its Nepal border area over fears that a barrier lake created during the initial landslide could trigger another disaster, after Wednesday’s catastrophic flooding in the region.

• Death toll climbs: At least 469 people have been killed in Nepal , according to the police. Dozens of Americans and other foreign nationals are among at least 1,300 people unaccounted for. Some missing foreigners have been rescued.

• On the ground: In Kathmandu , a CNN team witnessed families’ anguish and despair as they learn the worst news of their loved ones from lists and photos on a morgue wall . A separate CNN team closer to the disaster zone is documenting devastated neighborhoods .

• Colossal force: Scientists are still working to determine exactly what caused the disaster. New video showed where a large portion of glacier broke and plunged into the river below, triggering a fast-moving wave of water, pulverized ice and rock.

Officials in Nepal’s Rasuwa district have received a notice saying a lake has broken its banks, Narendra Pariyar, the most senior bureaucrat of the district, said Friday, Reuters news agency reported.

The official said he can see the water level rising.

Nepal has paused rescue operations for the next hour and 30 minutes, an army official said, Reuters reported.

China is suspending rescue efforts near Gyirong land port on the border with Nepal because of fears of another disastrous landslide or flood in the area, state media reports.

A barrier lake formed by Wednesday’s deluge has been rising over the past 48 hours, threatening to unleash another deadly flow of earth or water.

Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported late Friday morning the newly formed lake has begun overflowing non-stop, posing such a great risk that rescue teams cannot proceed to the hard-hit land port.

“We have no choice but to stop here for the time being,” said a CCTV reporter who is following the rescue efforts.

“Because the lake is continuing to overflow, there is a very real possibility that it could trigger new flash floods or landslides, so it is extremely dangerous to proceed to the areas that have been identified as priorities for search and rescue operations,” it said.

Most of the rescue team gathered at the entrance of Laojiang village in Gyirong Town, said CCTV. Laojiang village is around 4.35 miles from the China-Nepal border.

David Fisher, head of the International Federation of Red Cross for Nepal, told CNN’s Kaitlan Collins about the challenges his teams face amid worries of a secondary flood.

He said teams are currently only “scratching the surface of emergency needs,” emphasizing the sheer magnitude and scale of the disaster.

A video posted on social media showed a large boulder barreling down the Trishuli River in Nepal, illustrating the enormous force of the floodwaters.

Devastating images of flood victims line the walls of a morgue in Kathmandu as families search for missing relatives hoping for closure, CNN’s Will Ripley reported from Nepal’s capital.

Photos of body parts, tattoos, and other identifying features were displayed in a desperate attempt for families to identify their loved ones.

“There are men on the wall, there are women, there are young children… it’s just a terrible situation,” Ripley said.

More than 1,200 people have been registered as missing and just a few dozens are currently being treated in hospital .

All 67 people in a Richa Treks tour group were likely washed away in Wednesday’s flooding disaster on the Nepal-China border, the group’s director Sangay Gurung told a CNN team in Kathmandu.

“It was very unfortunate. They were at the Chinese customs and immigration, queuing up. And suddenly there was this big flash flood, ” Gurung said. “Everything got washed away on the Chinese side. The entire customs and immigration building.”

The group of 67 included 60 Indian nationals, five Americans, and two New Zealanders.

A second group, including eight foreign nationals and two staff, were in a bus and a guide directed them to run up a mountain, Gurung said. They were “very lucky” and are now safe in Nepal’s capital Kathmandu, he added.

Around 700 people were at the customs center when the flood hit, according to Gurung.

“We were totally shocked, we never thought in our wildest dreams that such a big catastrophe could happen.”

It’s Friday morning in the Nepal-China border region, where hundreds are dead and thousands remain missing after a catastrophic flood hit the area. CNN teams on the ground in flood-stricken Rasuwa are speaking with affected communities and rescue crews race to search for survivors.

Video geolocated by CNN showed a glacier breaking off a mountain and plunging into the river below. Scientists are working to establish the exact cause of the disaster.

Rescue efforts : The death toll from the catastrophic flooding rose to at least 469, Nepal police said Friday. A frantic search continues for more than 1,300 missing people, including dozens of Americans among at least 700 foreigners.

Secondary threat: Rain and chilly weather is expected in China’s Gyirong County, where it’s feared a dam created during the initial landslide could breach and cause more flooding.

Missing loved ones : Among those still awaiting news are the children of parents on a 60th birthday bucket-list trip, the brother of a woman and her daughter on a Himalayan adventure and the family of a couple on a once-in-a-lifetime pilgrimage .

Incoming aid: President Donald Trump said the US is ready to send “any help” to Nepal, joining the European Union and India among those announcing plans to provide humanitarian assistance.

CNN’s Alea Motwane, August Phillips, Laura Paddison and Lex Harvey contributed reporting.

CNN journalists are on the ground outside a hospital in Kathmandu, where families are lining up to register the names of their missing loved ones.

More than 1,200 people have been registered as missing in the flooding disaster, according to a local police officer operating the desk outside the Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital in Nepal’s capital.

Families are also checking paper notices taped to the wall listing 31 injured survivors who are being treated in the hospital.

Nepali filmmaker Tashi Bista has been using thermal drones to help with flood rescue efforts. He speaks to CNN’s Anderson Cooper about the devastating destruction he has seen and the challenges involved in finding survivors.

Video shared by a photographer on Chinese social media and geolocated by CNN captures where a large portion of glacier near Langtang Lirung peak broke along the Nepal-China border, causing a devastating avalanche and landslide.

In his post, the photographer wrote he heard the sound of the falling glacier around 10:30 a.m. local time on August 26, and at first mistook it for a military exercise.

Wednesday’s glacial collapse was so strong that it was initially reported by the US Geological Survey as a magnitude 4.4 earthquake.

Comparing satellite images from before and after the disaster, scientists have established that an enormous chunk of glacier sheared off from high on a mountain.

From there, it plunged to the river below — a roughly 7,000-foot vertical drop, a CNN analysis shows.

Though information on the volume of rock and ice that fell is not available yet, the section of the glacier that fell is approximately 2,000 feet wide, with a similarly sized section of rock next to it falling as well.

The sheared glacier left a 3,000-foot-wide gash in the mountainside, according to CNN analysis of satellite imagery.

The flood wave – a cascade of water, pulverized ice and rock – “descended the first 22 kilometers (13.7 miles) at an average speed of 193 kilometers per hour (120 mph),” said Jeffrey Kargel, a senior scientist at the Planetary Science Institute, a non-profit institute. That means it traveled nearly 14 miles in just 6 minutes and 50 seconds.

Scientists are still unpicking the exact causes of the devastating flooding.

New video posted on Chinese social media captures where a large portion of glacier near Langtang Lirung peak broke along the Nepal-China border, causing a devastating avalanche and landslide.

CNN’s Laura Paddison and Thomas Bordeaux contributed reporting.

The threat of further landslides and flooding along the devastated Nepal-China border is making a difficult search for survivors even more dangerous, the Red Cross told CNN.

“We’re extremely concerned about the possibility of a renewed flood, even as the authorities are working very, very hard to reopen roads that have been blocked for communities that have still not received significant assistance,” said David Fisher, Head of the International Federation of the Red Cross (IFRC) for Nepal.

Two days after the disaster, many people in the flood zone are “still very disoriented,” he said. Rescuers and volunteers are doing their best to distribute flood warnings to people still in shock, Fisher told CNN’s Kaitlan Collins.

“It’s critical that we reach both the existing emergency needs and that we get these warnings out as soon as possible,” he said.

A video posted to social media shows people trapped on the balcony of a building in Bidur, a town on the Trishuli River in Nepal, at the moment the devastating flooding swept through.

Akash and Rashika Sharma, the son and daughter of a New York-based couple missing in Nepal, sat down with Anderson Cooper and shared how a trip she and her brother encouraged their parents to take has now turned their world upside down.

Gyirong County, an area on the China-Nepal border that was severely affected by the landslide, is set to see more rain over the next three days, as authorities warn of future landslides and flooding .

Gyirong County will see frequent precipitation, with rainfall mostly light, Chinese state media CCTV reported, citing the China Meteorological Administration. Temperatures in the area may be as low as 8 degrees Celsius (46 degrees Fahrenheit), “making it feel relatively damp and chilly,” CCTV reported.

China’s Ministry of Resources earlier warned that there is a “high risk” a dam created during the landslide in Nepal could breach and cause more flooding downstream as a lake develops behind it.

This could potentially cause “renewed flooding and damage in downstream areas, including the Gyirong Port,” a major land border crossing between China and Nepal that was wiped out by the landslide, the ministry said in a statement.

It could pose risks to Chinese emergency responders dispatched to the port area for rescue missions.

The lake, known as a “barrier lake,” is forming near where Nepal’s Chhochen Khola river meets the Purepu Tsangpo river, which flows into China, the ministry said.

CNN’s director of international news and video Sugam Pokharel was supposed to visit loved ones in Nepal this December, but since catastrophic flooding swamped a China-Nepal border region he has had trouble getting in touch with some of the friends he is supposed to visit.

“This feels especially personal and difficult for me,” he told CNN on Thursday.

Pokharel was born and raised in Nepal before coming to the United States 20 years ago. He said he has many friends there that are unreachable after the catastrophic flooding.

“This is incredibly heartbreaking and worrying especially not knowing what has happened to them,” Pokharel said of his friends.

He said possible secondary flooding and decomposing carcasses pose a risk to residents.

“They’re saying, well, what do we do now? We don’t have our homes anymore, but do we shelter where we are staying right now? Or do we go to a like a higher altitude, essentially climb a hill and shelter in a forest?” he told CNN.

“There are so many livestock, so many dead animals… they’re going to start rotting soon. And so there’s a concern of an epidemic.”

Pokharel also noted that a major highway connecting Nepal’s capital Kathmandu is closed, potentially cutting off crucial supplies to residents.

“There is a cooking gas shortage in Kathmandu and the cooking gas comes in trucks from India,” he said. “And if the highway blockage continues for longer, the people in Kathmandu and other areas are also going to start feeling the pain soon.”

Additional police teams, some with drones, have been deployed across central Nepal amid frantic ongoing search and rescue efforts after landslide created devastating flooding.

The wave of water , pulverized ice and rocks tore through the steep mountain valleys on the Nepal-China border.

The torrent was loaded with silt, sand, gravel and boulders, which all moved together as a single fluid that Hatim Sharif, an engineering professor at the University of Texas at San Antonio, compared to “liquid cement.”

At the same speed, “this material hits a building with roughly twice the force of water,” Sharif said. The flood wave was able to carry with it “boulders the size of cars,” he added.

Its composition also makes rescue efforts more hazardous. The debris can hold water for a long time, making it “treacherously variable,” Sharif said. While one patch can bear a person’s weight, another can swallow them to their waist.

Depth is another issue. The sediment left behind is likely to be many feet thick in places, he added, meaning searching for people “is done by probing and by hand, and it is very slow.”

A big concern is that fresh rain could set everything moving again. “Downstream communities need to stay off the riverbanks even on days that look calm,” Sharif said.

Thunderstorms are possible for at least the next couple of days in the flood zone, as a notoriously wet seasonal weather pattern continues.

The region is in its monsoon season, so daily chances of rain are the norm. Some places could pick up multiple inches of rain in a few hours, while others see much less or even stay completely dry.

It’s difficult to pinpoint exactly where the most drenching downpours will occur, but the hardest-hit areas could experience them, which could challenge search and recovery efforts.

Nepal’s monsoon typically lasts from June through September. The country sees about 80% of its rainfall during this time .

Here’s what the radar looks like through Saturday, local time:

The flooding along the Chinese-Nepali border on Wednesday hit a popular route for pilgrims and tourists.

Summer often brings hundreds of Hindu, Buddhist, Jain and Bonpo pilgrims to the area around Mount Kailash, a Tibetan mountain revered in each religion. Pilgrims often walk around the distinctive, pyramid-shaped mountain on a roughly 30-mile, high-altitude trail. However, no climber has ever officially summited the mountain. The Chinese government has prohibited ascents due to the peak’s religious significance.

Numerous travel and trekking agencies offer packages guiding people between Nepal’s capital Kathmandu and Mount Kailash, though pilgrim access to the site has been disrupted numerous times in recent years due to the COVID-19 pandemic and political disputes between China and India.

The flooding hit an overland route between Kathmandu and Tibet frequented by many of these tour groups. One Indian guru said in a post on social media that 77 pilgrims guided by his organization were at the Chinese-Nepali border when the disaster began and remain unaccounted for.

President Donald Trump said the US has offered aid and support to Nepal following catastrophic floods that have left dozens of Americans missing.

“Oh, it’s terrible,” Trump said when asked Thursday afternoon about the flood and missing Americans. “We’ve called Nepal and we’ve offered any help that they need. You know, we have a very good relationship with Nepal and that was a brutal.”

“Nobody’s ever seen anything quite like that where very powerful, strong, well-built buildings were wiped out like they were toothpicks,” he added during an Oval Office event.

Trump went on to say that around 50 to 60 Americans are missing but said that he hasn’t received the full list yet.

“Hopefully they’re OK but that looked pretty — that looked like something that people will not be, somebody will be lost, unfortunately,” the president said.

CNN has reported that more than 1,300 people are missing following the floods in Nepal, including at least 700 foreigners from two dozen countries. The death toll in Nepal has climbed to more than 350 people.

articles.title: Indonesians march on parliament to demand crackdown on corruption
articles.summary: Thousands of Indonesians demand harsher penalties for corruption during protests outside parliament in Jakarta.
articles.body:
Thousands of Indonesians have marched on the parliament in Jakarta to demand harsher punishment for corrupt officials.

The protests on Thursday fell a year to the day since antigovernment rallies turned into riots in which about 10 people were killed and nearly 7,000 arrested.

Riot police held the crowd behind the locked gates of the legislature for much of the day.

The AFP news agency reported that after nightfall, some protesters threw objects at officers, who answered with tear gas and a water cannon. A police post and motorcycle were set alight and several people were carried off on stretchers, it added.

Students also marched in the cities of Yogyakarta and Makassar.

Protesters are demanding that parliament pass a bill, first brought before it in 2008, that would allow the state to seize assets tied to corruption. Some at the rally called for corrupt officials to face the death penalty.

Some lawmakers met with representatives of the protest group United Pati Community Alliance outside of parliament and promised to resign if the bill is not passed by December 15, according to its leader, Sopriyano.

Some 200 students from several universities were present at the protest, urging the government to scrap a free school meal programme marred by corruption claims and repeated food poisoning incidents.

They also called for an end to the “militarisation” of Indonesian society and lower food prices.

“We chose August 27 to commemorate because last year there were riots and various other incidents. And today we want to convey our aspirations, not cause riots,” a representative for the students told Reuters.

Jakarta police deployed 18,500 officers and detained 65 people before the march, on suspicion of being “provocateurs”, spokesperson Budi Hermanto said.

Chief Security Minister Djamari Chaniago said the deployment was not aimed at curbing their right to free expression.

“We will escort them so that their aspirations can be conveyed properly,” he said.

articles.title: Drug testing: Could services in Northern Ireland tackle substance issues?
articles.summary: With more than 250 drug-related deaths in Northern Ireland in 2024, is it time for a new approach?
articles.body:
Bars, chip vans and portaloos are all common sights at classic outdoor gigs in Northern Ireland.

But in the rest of the UK and the Republic of Ireland, some also have dedicated facilities that allow for the rapid testing and identification of harmful drugs and substances.

Police this week warned about the "serious, potentially life-changing, risks of taking or supplying illegal drugs" at outdoor music events.

Belfast City Council recently called for testing services to be brought in, but issues about laws and funding have resurfaced.

Samples of drugs are sent away and substances tested for their chemical make up and strength - but there are differences in how the results are communicated back to the public.

Some festivals in GB and the Republic of Ireland operate "back-of-house" testing . That's where substances, either found in searches or deposited in amnesty bins outside, are tested.

If something potentially dangerous is found, a warning will go out to festival goers and health officials on site.

Authorities and organisations who operate drug testing, as well as festivals, are clear they don't condone or encourage drug-taking, rather it is a harm reduction method.

Licences to operate services in Britain are given out by the Home Office , but in Northern Ireland licencing is devolved meaning the responsibility rests with the Department of Health's (DoH) Medicines Regulatory Group.

There's also "front-of-house" testing where individuals bring their substances to get tested and are not given them back.

Councillor Micky Murray brought a motion to Belfast City Council earlier this year calling for a pilot of drug and pill testing facilities at major events.

"We've always dealt with [drugs] as a policing issue but it's not a policing issue, we need to deal with it as a healthcare issue," he told BBC News NI.

"It's never worked, so it's time that we start something new."

There was pushback to harm reduction messaging published by the Public Health Agency earlier in the summer , with Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) MP Carla Lockhart stating: "The only responsible message on illegal drugs is simple: don't take them."

But Murray said not supporting harm reduction methods was putting people at risk.

"This isn't going to increase people taking drugs and increase life-long drug taking. What this will do is prevent deaths, prevent enormous harm to people which could be prevented by having the information on hand," he added.

"What we're doing now without giving people the information they need is doing more harm than providing them with the information that they need to make safer decisions."

In June, a report on the motion concluded there is "no legislative framework, funding mechanism or operational model in place" that would allow the council to run such facilities.

It added DoH officials advised no formal application for a licence has ever been received and there are a range of issues that would need to be addressed before it is considered .

DoH told BBC News NI it stands ready to support the council but "remains conscious of the resource, licensing, and legislative implications".

Some have argued such facilities normalise drug taking. But there are some who think they are vital.

Georgia Jones, 18, died following a cardiac arrest and a 50-minute fit after taking two MDMA pills - found to be roughly six-times stronger than usual - at Mutiny Festival in Portsmouth in 2018.

Her mum, Janine Milburn, said while she was aware her daughter had tried drugs before, she thinks testing services could have helped.

"In my eyes, it gives people another barrier so they decide they're going to take a substance, they maybe haven't done it before or only done it a couple of times, they don't really know what they're doing," she said.

"It gives them a professional to go to, but it also gives them another chance to say I'm not going to do it now."

Janine now runs a harm reduction charity, Georgia Jones Don't Go With The Flo , and often speaks to young people about the effects of drugs.

"They get all their information from movies, songs, from peers, so they're not getting that correct information and this is what is really damaging them," she added.

"Even if they're not taking it, they'll maybe be around people who are so they need to be given this information.

"Georgia took two pills and was found to be six-times over what you would expect to find, so it's these high doses and not necessarily the drug itself."

What lessons can NI learn from elsewhere?

The Loop already operates at some festivals in England as a harm reduction method, and tests surrendered substances "in real time" to find out what is in circulation and inform attendees and health officials within minutes.

Its Chief Executive Katy Porter, said they accept people are taking drugs but neither "condemn nor condone" it.

"We need clear information in order to equip people from a public health point of view to be able to make informed choices and informed decisions," she added.

"Every year there are a number of deaths within festivals and these are preventable."

In the last six months, tests on MDMA pills by The Loop have shown it's not the adulteration of substances that is causing concern, but the variable high strengths.

"One thing we want to get across to people is one pill is not a single dose, and when choosing to take them, you won't know the strength. They might look similar, but without testing we're unable to understand just by sight or looking at them what that strength is."

It's also a trend Professor Eamon Keenan from Ireland's Health Service Executive (HSE), is seeing.

The HSE's Safer Nightlife Programme involves back-of-house testing at festivals like Electric Picnic, and Keenan said there's been great results so far.

"Since we've started producing the harm reduction messages, there's a lot more trust and confidence from the young people who are happier to engage with our volunteers," he said.

From festival testing alone, Kennan said the HSE have got about 300 samples which has resulted in 14 risk messages being sent out and substances never before seen in Ireland being identified.

Keenan said the "bottom line" is that it is safer not to take drugs at all.

"But we're living in a reality where we do know that people take drugs, and its our job to identify the substances that are circulating and then advise people in the risks and harms associated with these drugs."

The reported successes are a blueprint of how services should roll out in Northern Ireland, expert Professor Anne Campbell said.

Campbell, from the Drug and Alcohol Research Network at Queen's University Belfast, said while drug testing exists in Northern Ireland, the results aren't circulated to the wider public.

According to Campbell, wastewater analysis shows a sharp rise in ketamine and cocaine being used in Northern Ireland - and the current laws promote a prohibitionist messaging.

"It's not helpful to tell people not to take drugs because we know that it does not work and we know from those within our treatment populations its definitely not working because of the rise in deaths year on year," he said.

"I think you need everybody to have a stake in this and really have an understanding as to how positive it can be."

articles.title: Deanshanger hedgehog charity to double capacity with new home
articles.summary: The charity, which currently rescues 250 hedgehogs a year, is moving to a new home in Buckingham.
articles.body:
A hedgehog rescue charity has raised £45,000 for a new home that will double the number of animals it can care for.

Rachel and Dominic Matthews currently run Deanshanger Hedgehog Rescue from sheds at separate locations on the Northamptonshire-Buckinghamshire border, where they look after about 250 of the creatures each year.

The charity's new home will be a modular building at Manor Farm, near Buckingham, and is expected to open in early 2027.

Rachel said: "The main reason we set up this project is because we get full every year, so this will double our capacity, not only in rehabilitation but also in our ICU."

The charity explained that it had been operating at capacity since June, admitting a new hedgehog as soon as another was discharged.

At the new location, they will be able to combine the rehab and the ICU, while also having space for outdoor pens.

Initially they expected the new building to cost about £50,000, but the charity found it could reduce the cost by using a modular building, which could also be moved if it needed to relocate.

Rachel added: "We didn't dream that we would get there as quickly as we have, because obviously it was a lot of money for us to raise.

"It seemed like such a lot of money at the start and I really didn't know whether we would actually do it, but in the last six months it rocketed... So thank you for everyone that supported us."

articles.title: Matt Lucas and Hugh Bonneville call for law on AI voice clones
articles.summary: The performers are asking the government to give every person in the UK a legal right to own their voice.
articles.body:
Actors including Matt Lucas, Hugh Bonneville and Nicola Coughlan have written to the UK government demanding greater protection against their voices being used by AI.

The performers are asking Prime Minister Andy Burnham to introduce legislation which would give every person in the UK a legal right to own their voice.

Voice clones are created by training AI on recordings of real people. Quick versions can be made in minutes from a few seconds of audio, but high-quality copycats tend to require hours.

Audiobook narrator Alice Sockett, who co-founded the campaign, called it "an existential threat to our entire industry".

"My voice is out there in the public domain but completely unprotected," she said.

"We're seeing voice theft increase every week."

A government spokesperson told the BBC that, while "digital replicas can be a powerful tool, including for the creative industries," there was also possibility for harm.

"We value and protect human creators, and that is why we have announced we will launch a consultation on how we address these harms, while protecting legitimate innovation", the spokesperson said.

More than 80 performers have signed the letter, with Derry Girls actor Siobhán McSweeney saying she was "deeply worried" that the government was lagging behind.

"There is a way to work alongside AI and to use it as a tool that benefits us rather than rendering us obsolete," she said.

"Our audiences want that human connection. Not AI."

As well as actors, other signatories include those working in other performing industries.

That includes Scottish singer Sandi Thom, known for her 2006 hit I Wish I Was a Punk Rocker (With Flowers in My Hair).

She said she was signing the letter because her voice was "unique to me and was handed to me at birth".

"Behind that voice is the emotion, the life, the pain, the tears and joy that I've felt along the way," she said.

It comes a few months after lawyers warned UK legislation has become "unfit for purpose" because of the advancements of AI tech.

"The law comes close, but it doesn't fully protect your voice, your face or your identity," Dr Mathilde Pavis said in June .

However, some people - for example those who are unable so speak properly because of illness - have welcomed technology that can replicate a person's voice.

Yvonne Johnson, who lost her voice due to motor neurone disease, told the BBC's Tech Life programme in February how having it cloned by AI had "totally blown her mind", and brought her closer to her family, who had forgotten what she sounded like.

Others have gone a step further and used AI not only to replicate a person's voice, but to create a holographic representation of them.

Pam Cronrath, from Washington state, used the tech to surprise mourners at her husband's funeral, where a digital version of her deceased partner addressed those who attended his wake.

"I was completely impressed," she told BBC News . "It stayed with me."

articles.title: Two vacant Connecticut office buildings built in 1980 and 1982 will become 286 apartments in a $120 million conversion, reusing 511,000 sq ft instead of tearing them down
articles.summary: US News: A pair of vacant office buildings in Connecticut have been acquired for redevelopment as multifamily housing. In a joint venture between developers Sa.
articles.body: A pair of vacant office buildings in Connecticut have been acquired for redevelopment as multifamily housing. In a joint venture between developers Saber-Hightower LLC and Granoff Real Estate, 101 and 201 Merritt 7, in the Merritt 7 office park in the New York City suburb of Norwalk, Connecticut, will be the sites of the project. While the acquisition price was not publicly disclosed, the project is budgeted at $120 million, according to a report by WRE News.The two buildings are eight-storeys long and encompass 511,000 square feet with more than 1,300 parking spaces. They will be transformed into 286 loft-style apartments, with the first units expected to be available as soon as 2027. Among these, 26 units will be designated affordable under Norwalk's inclusionary requirements. The unit mix comprises 42 studios, 167 one-bedrooms, and 77 two-bedrooms, averaging 983 square feet. Most units include dens suitable for home offices, nurseries, or storage. Built in 1980 and 1982, the site carries an as-of-right residential density of up to 564 units, but Saber-Hightower’s plan calls for 286 loft-style units, under Norwalk's 2023 comprehensive rezoning.Moreover, the properties will also receive a resort-style amenity area featuring a swimming pool with cabanas, dog runs, a putting green and a bocce court. Bank OZK has provided a $ 75.5 million senior construction loan to support the conversion of the buildings. The two eight-story buildings were the first of six built in the Merritt 7 office park, at the northeast corner of the Merritt Parkway and Route 7. Both buildings are steps from the Merritt 7 Metro-North station on the Danbury Branch, giving residents rail access to Stamford, Greenwich, and Manhattan alongside direct highway connections.Rather than tearing down the buildings, they are being rebuilt for space and opportunity. “While some developers may have looked at these buildings as a teardown-and-rebuild opportunity, we saw the value in reusing what was there,” said Greg Belew, co-founder of Saber-Hightower. “With 11-foot ceilings, wall-to-wall windows, and simple floor plates, it was apparent to us that we had great bones to work with. The best approach to adaptive reuse is to keep it simple. We are making no structural modifications to either building, and that lets us control costs and mitigate risk.”"Because we had so much space to work with, we can give residents more generously sized layouts than a ground-up building would allow," said Marty Berger, co-founder of Saber-Hightower. "There is unmet demand in this market for residents who want a more sophisticated experience."Last January, the other four buildings within the Merritt 7 office park were sold for $58.5 million. That portion of the office park includes the headquarters for companies including Xerox, Terex, Emcor, Hearst Connecticut Media Group, Common Fund, Datto/Kaseya, MBI, and LBB Specialities.Saber-Hightower, led by Marty Berger and Greg Belew, formed the partnership with Granoff Real Estate, an affiliate of Granoff Architects, which serves as project architect. Granoff Architects designed the conversion of The Mill in the Glenville section of Greenwich; a 1980s office building and adjacent historic mill converted to residential; the property traded for $97.5 million in 2025."The Saber-Hightower and Granoff teams integrated seamlessly as true co-developers," said Rich Granoff, founder and managing principal of Granoff Real Estate. "Given continued weakness in regional suburban office markets, we look forward to exploring other conversion opportunities with Saber-Hightower."Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2005, carpenter Isaiah Robertson began covering his Niagara Falls home inside and out with brightly painted religious art; after his 2020 death, the house was preserved and is now open for guided tours
articles.summary: US News: In 2005, Isaiah Henry Robertson, a Jamaican-born carpenter and devout Christian living in Niagara Falls, New York, began transforming his modest house.
articles.body: In 2005, Isaiah Henry Robertson, a Jamaican-born carpenter and devout Christian living in Niagara Falls, New York, began transforming his modest house into what he believed was a preparation site for the Second Coming of Jesus Christ. Convinced that God had told him the world would end in 2014, Robertson spent years covering nearly every surface of his home, inside and out, with intricate, brightly painted wooden religious art. After his death in 2020, the property was acquired by the Kohler Foundation, gifted to the Niagara Falls National Heritage Area, and preserved as a community landmark. Today, visitors can explore 'Prophet Isaiah’s Second Coming House' on guided tours that highlight his faith-driven artistry and legacy. Read on to learn more about this unusual incident, as described on the Niagara Falls National Heritage Area’s official pages about the house and its tours.A carpenter guided by faithIsaiah Robertson was just twelve when his mother told him she had received a vision that he would do great things. Raised in Jamaica, he was taught to pray for salvation and, following what he saw as Jesus’ example, became a carpenter. He later claimed to have built his first house without formal training, relying instead on faith and practical skill.At 24, Robertson moved to Canada and continued working in construction. In 2004, he relocated to Niagara Falls, New York, where he renovated and resold houses. His church, Mount Erie Baptist Church, hired him to sheetrock and panel walls. Still, instead of standard materials, he used natural oak and covered the walls and cathedral ceiling with intricate, interlocking wood cutouts depicting religious imagery. He said God instructed him to use oak, and he purchased the wood with his entire life savings.Preparing for the end of the worldIn 2005, Robertson said God spoke to him again with a new directive: transform his own home because the end of the world was coming in 2014. He began by building a 25-foot kaleidoscopic cross near the driveway, decorated with hundreds of multichrome wooden armatures. At the front of the house, he mounted a 300-pound boulder from Three Sisters Island in Niagara Falls State Park, where he believed the Rapture would take place.Robertson’s vision was both personal and public. He believed that eternally damned souls flying past his house would see the cross and have one last chance to repent and be saved. Roadside America has described the house as “a spectacular piece of spiritual eye candy,” covered in thousands of bright-hued, hand-carved surfaces featuring multi-denominational religious symbols such as doves, trumpets, crescents, multi-pointed stars and “wheels within wheels.” Robertson often said that God guided his hands as he worked, and he even interpreted an accidental brush stroke near the front door as an image of the Virgin Mary.Inside the spiritual sanctuaryInside, Robertson created a dedicated prayer room, covering the floors with candles and symbolic purple bead patterns that he said represented “the path to Salvation.” Every available surface, be it walls, ceilings, doors and trim, was adorned with hand-carved and painted motifs drawn from Christian iconography and his own spiritual visions.The result is less a conventional house and more a three-dimensional devotional artwork, a physical expression of Robertson’s belief that Niagara Falls, one of the natural wonders of the world, would be the site of Christ’s return. For him, the house was not just a home but a spiritual sanctuary and a signpost for the faithful and the lost alike.From private vision to public landmarkIsaiah Robertson passed away in January 2020 at the age of 72. Friends and neighbours remembered him as warm and welcoming, as well as a talented woodworker and artist whose faith shaped every aspect of his life.In 2021, the Kohler Foundation purchased the house and gifted it to the Niagara Falls National Heritage Area (NFNHA). The organisation began the work of preserving the structure and restoring its art, with the long-term goal of transforming the site into a community space that tells Robertson’s story and inspires more community art through events and programs.Visiting the house todayToday, the property is known as Prophet Isaiah’s Second Coming House and is open to the public through guided tours run by the Niagara Falls National Heritage Area. The 90-minute tour takes visitors through both the interior and exterior of the house, including areas not visible from the street, offering a close-up look at Robertson’s evolving masterpiece.Guides discuss intuitive art, religious symbolism, the challenges of preserving outdoor folk art, and what it means to leave a spiritual and creative legacy in the heart of a community. Tours are priced at $15 for adults, with free admission for children under 18, and meet at 1308 Ontario Ave. in Niagara Falls, New York.For many visitors, the house is more than a curiosity; it is a testament to one man’s unwavering belief that his art could serve a higher purpose. In a city known for its natural spectacle, Prophet Isaiah’s home adds another layer of wonder—a human-made shrine born of faith, craftsmanship and a vision of the end times that never came, yet left something enduring behind.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Six months of war between Iran, US leave Arab states facing tough questions
articles.summary: The Iran war is settling into attrition, with no regime collapse and Gulf economies facing growing uncertainty.
articles.body:
Analysts broadly agree the United States and Israel’s war on Iran will not see regime collapse in Tehran or a definite victory for Washington, but rather a dragged-out affair of stagnation and attrition.

The hope among the US leadership at the start of the war, which began after surprise Israeli and US attacks on February 28, was that mounting economic and military pressure on Iran would force a structural shift in Tehran. Six months on, it is clear this vision will not come about, and instead many are preparing for a protracted war and managed fallout.

Oil-dependent economies are still absorbing supply shocks after traffic in the Strait of Hormuz slowed to a trickle of pre-war levels following Iran’s attacks on shipping and a US blockade on Iranian ports.

The US military is still entrenched in a region that remains its most militarised in years. Although the war’s intensity has lessened since a memorandum of understanding (MoU) was signed by Washington and Tehran in June, there is no sign it will conclude, leading to continued uncertainty about the future.

Existing tensions, such as those between the Houthi rebels and Saudi Arabia in Yemen, look only set to increase as the war drags on. The influence of rival powers, such as those of India and China, remains stalled rather than stopped, with Beijing’s Belt and Road Initiative having already established itself within the Middle East and North Africa. All in all, the region remains in flux where formal alliances with outside powers no longer guarantee safety.

The defence agreement between Turkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia recently signed in Mecca will likely be the first of many such military pacts agreed in the region.

“The war has just accelerated trends, but hasn’t really started anything that wasn’t already under way. The Gulf countries were already diversifying their economies,” Sanam Vakil, director of the Middle East and North Africa Programme at Chatham House, told Al Jazeera. “Many were already looking at broadening their defence partnerships beyond existing US security guarantees, as well as increasing their own defence capability.”

Israel, for its part, is still pursuing its regional project of “paramountcy”, HA Hellyer of the Royal United Services Institute said, despite its failure to bring Iran to its knees this year.

“There is no chance of the government in Tehran falling in the next six months,” Hellyer told Al Jazeera. “If everything were to theoretically stay the same … with just increased economic pressure, that could eventually cause a ripple effect that could lead to state collapse in Iran. But we’re talking years, not months, and everything is not likely to stay the same.”

The effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz and strikes on regional cities have hindered Gulf states’ plans to use oil revenues as an engine to diversify their economies and build on their reputations as a safe haven to encourage investors.

Shipments of oil, derivative products and liquefied natural gas (LNG) have been repeatedly and severely disrupted since the US and Israel launched their attacks on Iran in February.

Transit through the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, which saw attacks on shipping by the Houthis during Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, became even more hazardous in July, when the Iran-allied Houthis declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia.

“The price of oil has increased broadly in line with the Gulf states’ difficulties in exporting it,” John Sfakianakis, chief economist at the Gulf Research Center, told Al Jazeera. “Is this going to go for six months? Is it going to go on for longer?”

Exacerbating the Gulf states’ difficulties is that, although the price of oil has risen, so has inflation. In addition to the economic difficulties the war has created, there is also growing pressure for Gulf states to invest more in defence.

For now, the majority of the states caught in the middle will look at ways of living with the turmoil and managing the consequences.

articles.title: Nepal-Tibet flood live updates: Rescue teams search for survivors as hundreds remain missing
articles.summary: Follow live updates as rescue teams search for survivors of catastrophic flash floods in Nepal and China, where 90 Americans are among hundreds of people unaccounted for.
articles.body:
What to know At least 469 people are dead after catastrophic flash floods Wednesday along the border between Nepal and China's Tibet region, Nepal police said. Hundreds of foreign tourists are among those who remain missing in the area, which is popular with trekkers and pilgrims. In China, where a mudslide hit a land crossing between Nepal and Tibet’s Gyirong county, authorities said three people were dead, two were rescued and 558 others were missing, including 260 foreigners. The State Department says 90 Americans are unaccounted for in Nepal and China, while three have been rescued in Nepal. It said it was not aware of any U.S. deaths. Rescue teams are using military helicopters, heavy machinery and dogs to search for survivors after the surging floodwaters washed out roads, buildings and bridges, cutting off thousands of people. Nepal and China have both warned of further flood risk as two lakes that have formed on either side of their border threaten to collapse. The deadly torrent followed a glacial collapse in the Himalayan region, which is home to many of the world's highest peaks and a high concentration of glaciers. While the exact cause of the disaster has yet to be determined, experts say climate change is causing glaciers to melt faster, increasing the risk of flooding and landslides.

articles.title: Groom seeks helicopter ride from wedding to play at Lord's
articles.summary: Peter Melhuish needs to captain his cricket team less than 24 hours after he ties the knot.
articles.body:
A groom is trying to secure a helicopter ride so he can play in a dream cricket match at Lord's immediately after his wedding in North Wales.

Peter Melhuish, from Guildford in Surrey, is due to play at Lord's on 6 September for his club Blackheath after they made it to the final of the Cawston Press Village Cup.

But the team captain is marrying his fiancée, Izzy Upton, in North Wales less than 24 hours earlier.

The couple, both 32, planned their wedding for the Saturday after Blackheath's local league fixtures finished for the season.

However, they did not factor in the club's success in the Village Cup, a nationwide tournament played on Sundays by local teams across the UK.

Now, Melhuish's clubmates are trying to raise around £9,000 so the pair can make the one-hour flight from North Wales to London by the game's 11:00 BST start.

"It'd be amazing if we can afford it and pull something together," said Melhuish.

"The only other way is a 5am taxi down from the wedding which wouldn't be much fun.

"It's amazing how the club are pulling together and helping us with it.

"It's really nice to have that support from them," he added.

Blackheath - which Melhuish first joined aged six - has entered the Village Cup since the tournament was first launched in 1972.

Melhuish added his fiancée Izzy had been "great".

"We've been organising the wedding for well over a year so the fixtures for the Village Cup hadn't even come out when we started organising it.

"She's been really supportive and very understanding of how much it means, not just to me but the club too," he continued.

articles.title: Why has Prospect strike action closed Norwich Airport today?
articles.summary: No flights are coming in or out of the airport as air traffic controllers strike for 24 hours.
articles.body:
Norwich Airport has been closed due to industrial action by air traffic control staff, causing disruption to hundreds of passengers. But how did it get to this point, what are union members unhappy with and what does it mean for people travelling?

Air traffic control members of the union Prospect voted in favour of strike action earlier this month.

It said its members were paid "significantly less than the UK market rate and have substandard maternity and paternity cover", and demanded the airport make improvements.

Starting on 17 August, members have commenced action short of a strike - which means staff work strictly to contracts and there is no swapping of shifts or non-contractually obligated overtime.

On 18 August, Prospect announced its members would take one day of strike action on 28 August after the airport had failed "to make a new offer to attempt to resolve the dispute".

There have already been some cancellations and disruption this month, but the union said this had been "occurring regularly even when industrial action is not taking place and is caused by a chronic shortage of personnel".

What did the union say ahead of the strike?

Prospect said talks were held with the airport on Wednesday, but the offer it was given "still fell well short of demands making it impossible for a shift" in its position.

David Avery, Prospect national secretary, said members "have no choice but to continue with strike action as planned".

"We appreciate that this will cause disruption for some passengers but when an employer treats staff with so little respect they have no option but to stick to their guns," he said.

"Norwich Airport can avert further strike action but they have to give us an offer which is competitive with the rest of the country.

"We are no longer prepared to provide the goodwill upon which the airport has been operating."

The strike will go on for 24 hours on Friday, meaning no flights will operate to or from the airport for the entirety of the day.

The airport said airlines had been informed and passengers should check with them about the latest information for their flights.

TUI, KLM, Ryanair and Loganair all operate out of the airport.

A TUI spokesperson said it was aware of the strikes and had "made the necessary preparations to ensure our customers can enjoy their holidays as planned".

It said its customers would be informed and it was expected some passengers would instead be flown from Southend Airport in Essex.

KLM said passengers who were unable to fly would be rebooked.

A Ryanair spokesperson said it did not expect any disruption to its operations while Loganair has been approached for comment.

The airport is also home to the East Anglian Air Ambulance, which confirmed the action would have "minimal impact on our ability to provide critical care".

A Norwich Airport spokesperson said it had made a substantial and responsible offer to Prospect members.

It had given a 3.5% pay increase in April and was now offering a further 3% consolidated increase from July, with another 3% from April next year.

It said this was alongside an additional 2% retention allowance, that employees could choose to direct into their pension through salary sacrifice.

"The employees concerned have received pay increases totalling approximately 25% over the past three years, and our benchmarking shows our latest offer would result in most roles being paid at or above the average for comparable regional airports," the spokesperson said.

"Prospect is also seeking four weeks' paid paternity leave and enhanced maternity provision for this group.

"Introducing benefits for one small group that are not available to the wider workforce would not be fair or financially sustainable for Norwich Airport."

They added that the union had "not provided constructive feedback" and its offer remained available.

articles.title: Nepal-Tibet floods: 'High risk' of lake bursting and causing second flood, warns China
articles.summary: China says a lake formed after a recent landslide near the Nepal-Tibet border may burst in the coming days.
articles.body:
China has warned there is a "high risk" that a lake which formed after the recent landslide near the Nepal-Tibet border may burst, causing a second flood downstream.

The warning comes after Wednesday's deadly flash flood in the same area which scientists say was triggered by the collapse of a mountain glacier into a river .

As of Friday morning, an estimated 2.5 million cubic metres of water had accumulated at the barrier lake, according to state broadcaster CCTV. A barrier lake is a body of water formed when debris dams up a river.

Officials said that three million cubic metres of water is expected to flow into the lake between Thursday and Saturday, posing a "high risk of breach".

The barrier lake, which formed at the confluence of the Chhochen Khola and Purepu Tsangpo rivers, has already started to overflow, according to China's Ministry of Water Resources. The area has also seen heavy rain.

Authorities have sent engineering teams to monitor the lake's water levels and the atmospheric conditions.

A CCTV report on Friday morning said that most of the Chinese emergency services were stuck at a village about 7km (4 miles) from Gyirong Port, the major land crossing linking Nepal and China which was hit by Wednesday's massive flood.

This was because the barrier lake was "overflowing non-stop" which could lead to fresh floods or debris flows.

Due to the risks, search and rescue operations had to be suspended near the Nepal-Tibet border, according to the report.
